sentence: This regime corresponds to the practical envelope of contemporary on-device deployment.
cited: No citation attached to this sentence.
why_unsupported: Asserts that the 1.7-7.2B band is what is actually deployed on device today. The study selected this band for tractability and hardware reasons; it measures nothing about deployment practice, and no source is offered for the envelope.
proposed_fix: State the selection rationale instead: "This regime was chosen because models of this size can be loaded and evaluated on a single 32 GB GPU and are the sizes released for on-device use by their publishers [2], [3]."

verdict.reasoning:
I tried all four refutation routes and none of them survives contact with the text.

**(1) "It's about the study's own design, not the world."** Fails. The sentence sits in §1.4 under "Model regime," and the three sentences before it *are* pure design statements ("The primary matched pairs sit in the roughly two-to-four-billion-parameter range... so the study spans approximately 1.7 to 7.2 billion parameters"). The target sentence then pivots outward and predicates something of the world — what "contemporary on-device deployment" practically encompasses. A rationale sentence that justifies a scope choice with a world-claim still asserts the world-claim. The study measures nothing about deployment practice.

**(2) "A citation on that sentence establishes it."** Fails. Confirmed at the source: `scripts/build_fyp_report_v6.js:424` renders the bullet with no bracket at all, while its immediate neighbours in the same chapter carry [1]–[6]. The string is verbatim unchanged since `scripts/build_fyp_report.js:355` (v1), i.e. it predates the citation-hardening pass that annotated the rest of Chapter 1. It is a legacy assertion that the hardening pass skipped.

**(3) "The surrounding context scopes it."** Fails, and in fact the context cuts the other way. §1.1 grounds only that "the smallest members of these families are sized for consumer hardware, mobile chipsets, and edge accelerators [2], [3]" and that quantization frameworks target edge inference [5]. Neither establishes an *envelope* — a bounded band identified with current on-device deployment. The band doesn't hold at either end on the report's own citations: [2] is Llama-3.2 including the 1B Instruct, below the study's 1.7B floor, so 1.7–7.2B does not bound the on-device space from below either. §2.3 likewise supports "below four billion... positioned for deployment at practical, resource-constrained scale" — it says nothing putting 7.2B in the envelope.

**(4) "It's a definition, or adequately hedged."** Fails. "Corresponds to **the** practical envelope of **contemporary** on-device deployment" is definite, present-tense, and unhedged — no "broadly," "approximately," "is commonly described as." It defines nothing; it asserts a correspondence between an empirically-chosen band and a real-world regime.

The decisive point is the report's own internal standard. Twice — §1.1 ("How often an end user in fact receives a quantized rather than a full-precision checkpoint is not something this study measures, and no prevalence figure is claimed for it") and §2.3 ("How widely each path is used in practice is not measured here, and no prevalence figure is claimed for it") — the author explicitly disclaims exactly this genre of deployment-practice claim. This one sentence makes the claim flatly and unsourced. Under D56 the fitness question is whether a source entails the sentence; here there is no source on it, and the nearest cited material entails a strictly weaker proposition.

The band's upper bound was in fact set by what the cross-family extension reached (Mistral-7B, chosen to fit the TC1 6h/10GB envelope), so the sentence has the post-hoc structure the auditor names: a range fixed by tractability, re-described as a fact about the world.

Severity is low — it is a motivational scoping sentence, touches no result or conclusion, and no downstream claim rests on it. Per D56 ("prefer the fix that adds rigour"), the fix is a reword plus citation rather than deletion, e.g. "This regime is the one that compression research targets for on-device inference [5], [7]" (which §1.1 already establishes), or an explicit hedge plus the same prevalence disclaimer already used in §1.1 and §2.3. sentence: The effect is also not bit-width-graded, in that a 128-token apparent increase in the smallest model does not replicate at the reference budget (Section 6.12).
defect_class: (f) absence of evidence stated as evidence of absence (with a supporting clause that does not support it)
cited: Internal cross-reference to Section 6.12; no external citation.
why_unsupported: Two problems. (i) "is not bit-width-graded" asserts the absence of a gradient; the study reports non-significant contrasts, which licenses "no bit-width gradient was detected", not that none exists — unless an equivalence test is quoted. (ii) The justification given varies the *generation-token budget* (128 vs 512), not the bit width, so it cannot bear on bit-width grading at all; the fp16 -> INT8 -> NF4 comparison is the relevant evidence and is not the one cited here.
proposed_fix: Separate the two claims and hedge the null: "No bit-width gradient is detected across fp16, INT8 and NF4 (Section 6.11). Separately, the 128-token apparent increase in the smallest model does not replicate at the 512-token reference budget (Section 6.12)."

verdict.reasoning:
I attempted refutation on all four permitted grounds and each fails.

**The warrant clause cites the wrong experiment (the auditor's prong (ii) is objectively correct).** I read both sections. §6.11 ("INT8 Precision Point: Method- and Bit-Width Sensitivity, fp16 to INT8 to NF4") is the ONLY place bit width is varied, and it is not the section cited. §6.12 is titled "Generation-Length Robustness: the 512-Token Rerun" and varies max_new_tokens only. The "128-token apparent increase in the smallest model" is Qwen3-1.7B's NF4 ΔASR +0.055 → 0.000 (Table 6.5), a single pair at a single bit width whose collapse is attributed to truncation ("roughly 60% of all responses were provably cut off"). That fact cannot bear on whether degradation is graded across fp16 → INT8 → NF4. The mismatch is confirmed by the report's own careful phrasing everywhere else, which keeps two conjuncts paired with two separate evidence streams: §6.11 concludes "neither bit-width-graded nor budget-robust" immediately after the INT8 nulls; Ch. 9 writes "neither bit-width-graded nor stable across generation budgets" after the INT8 evidence. The Introduction compressed this, kept conjunct 1 (bit width) and evidence stream 2 (budget), and welded them with "in that". Supplying a specific wrong warrant is worse than supplying none, because it misdirects a verifier.

A charitable rescue also fails on the facts: the 128-token signal that was INT8-specific and non-monotonic (rose at INT8, reverted at NF4 — the actual bit-width-grading evidence) belongs to **Llama-3.2-3B**, not the smallest model (§6.11, Appendix I.11). So the sentence cannot be read as a garbled reference to the INT8 result either — wrong model and wrong section.

**"Adequately hedged" fails, and the report itself proves the standard (prong (i)).** "The effect is also not bit-width-graded" is flat and unhedged. §6.11 explicitly states the correct epistemic rule — "Absence of significance is not by itself evidence of equivalence, so the same ten contrasts were also submitted to a two-one-sided-tests (TOST) equivalence procedure [49]" — but that TOST covers **capability only**. On the safety axis there is no equivalence test; Ch. 8 concedes the safety null is MDE-bounded at 0.04–0.09 ΔASR and "should therefore be read as bounded... rather than showing that the change is exactly zero." So the assertive "is not" wording on the safety axis is exactly the move the report disallows one section earlier, minus the TOST that licensed it there.

**"About the study's own data/design" does not save it.** That refutation applies when an auditor mistakes an internal result for a world-claim. Here the defect is internal warrant-to-claim mismatch, which survives it — and the sentence sits in the §1.5 Contributions list, where it reads as a general finding about quantization.

Fix that adds rigour rather than deleting (per D56): split the conjuncts and attach each to its own evidence, e.g. "No bit-width gradient was detected: every INT8 harmful-compliance contrast is non-significant under both judges across all five pairs (Section 6.11). Nor is the effect budget-robust — a 128-token apparent increase in the smallest model does not replicate at the reference budget (Section 6.12)." Optionally note that the safety null is bounded by the per-pair MDE, since no TOST was run on that axis.

sentence: The existence of OR-Bench nevertheless establishes that over-refusal is now treated as a first-class safety axis rather than a footnote.
cited: Attached by reference to [19] OR-Bench in the preceding sentences.
why_unsupported: "Establishes" over-claims what one benchmark can show. The existence of a single dedicated benchmark demonstrates that its authors treat over-refusal as a first-class axis; it does not establish how the field at large now treats it. The verb is the problem — the sentence asserts entailment from one artifact to a community-wide norm.
proposed_fix: "OR-Bench nevertheless shows that over-refusal is now the subject of dedicated, large-scale benchmarks in its own right."

verdict.reasoning:
I tried to refute this and could not. Location: `scripts/build_fyp_report_v6.js:459` (§2.2; also present in `scripts/build_rewritten_fyp_report_v1.py`; NOT in v5).

Each refutation route fails:

1. **Not about the study's own data/design.** The predicate is "over-refusal *is now treated as* a first-class safety axis" — a claim about how the research community behaves, not about this study's instrument choice. The instrument-choice claims sit in the *preceding* sentences ("XSTest is retained as the instrument here because...").

2. **Not hedged.** "Nevertheless" is a concessive connector that pivots away from the XSTest-retention justification; it does not modalise the field claim that follows. The verb is "establishes" — the strongest available entailment verb, with no "suggests", "indicates", or "is one sign that". The subject is explicitly "The existence of OR-Bench", i.e. the sentence names a single artifact as the ground for a community-wide norm.

3. **The citation does not establish the proposition.** [19] is OR-Bench itself (Cui et al., ICML 2025 — a real archival venue, so no evidence-grade problem). But a benchmark paper is evidence of what *its authors* built; it cannot be its own evidence for how the field at large now organises safety axes. The auditor's attribution-mismatch reading is grammatically exact.

4. **Not a definition.** "First-class safety axis rather than a footnote" is a characterisation of collective research practice, not a stipulation of terms.

Two further points that push this from arguable to clear:

- **Internal tension with the report's own §2.1.** Three paragraphs earlier the report enumerates the field's flagship multi-dimensional frameworks and their axes: TrustLLM's six (truthfulness, safety, fairness, robustness, privacy, machine ethics), DecodingTrust's six (toxicity, stereotype bias, robustness, privacy, machine ethics, fairness), SafetyBench. Over-refusal is a top-level axis in none of them. The report's own survey therefore undercuts "first-class safety axis", even if it supports the weaker "not a footnote".
- **The author's own demonstrated standard, ten lines later.** §2.3 says of a comparable general-practice claim: "How widely each path is used in practice is not measured here, and no prevalence figure is claimed for it." The same document shows the author knows exactly how to scope this class of statement; the OR-Bench sentence is unscoped by omission, not by design.

Strongest counter-argument, for the record (it changes severity, not the verdict): "footnote" is a low bar, and an 80k-prompt dedicated benchmark evaluating 32 models across 8 families, peer-reviewed at ICML, genuinely does rule out "marginal afterthought". If the predicate were only "not a footnote", I would call this refuted. It is not — "first-class safety axis" claims parity with harmful-compliance in the field's measurement practice, and one benchmark cannot carry that.

Severity: low, wording-level, conclusion-neutral. It touches no result, no number, and no RQ verdict. The rigour-adding fix per D56 is to reattribute rather than delete — e.g. "OR-Bench's scale, and its publication at ICML, indicate that over-refusal now supports dedicated large-scale measurement rather than being a side observation" — which keeps the point, drops the one-artifact→norm entailment, and would clear an `epistemic_hedge` trigger by rewording rather than by weakening a pattern.

sentence: However, the CPU path is not used for quantized runs, because BitsAndBytes requires a CUDA device.
cited: No citation attached to this sentence.
why_unsupported: Stated as a property of the library in general. bitsandbytes device support is version-dependent (non-CUDA backends have since been added), so the unqualified "requires a CUDA device" is an over-general claim; what the study can attest to is the behaviour of the pinned version in its environment, plus its own loader's refusal to quantize on CPU.
proposed_fix: "However, the CPU path is not used for quantized runs: in the pinned bitsandbytes version used here, 4-bit loading requires a CUDA device."

verdict.reasoning:
I could not refute it. The sentence splits into a scoped design fact and an unscoped external-software claim, and only the first survives.

WHAT IS LEGITIMATE: "the CPU path is not used for quantized runs" is a verified property of the study's own pipeline. /Users/tanueihorng/fyp_quant/ethical_benchmark/models/loader.py:219-222 raises a RuntimeError whenever spec.quantized is true and the resolved runtime device is not 'cuda', and the next paragraph of Ch. 3.3 says exactly that ("Four-bit loading is forbidden on a CPU runtime. The loader raises a clear error...").

WHAT OVER-REACHES: the causal clause "because BitsAndBytes requires a CUDA device" is stated in bare present tense as a property of the library itself, with no version qualifier and no citation. It converts a design choice into an external necessity. bitsandbytes device support is version-dependent (non-CUDA backends, including a CPU backend for 4-bit inference, were added after the 0.43 era), so the unqualified form is over-general and plausibly already false for a build co-installed with this report's stack.

EACH REFUTATION ROUTE FAILS:
(1) "It is about the study's own design" - only the main clause is; the reason clause asserts a library-general capability, not an environment fact.
(2) "Adequately scoped by context" - the neighbouring paragraph describes the loader's refusal (the correctly scoped statement) but follows rather than qualifies the general claim, and Chapter 4 repeats the unqualified version verbatim: "a four-bit path that BitsAndBytes does not support" (04_chapter_4_system_design_and_implem.txt:77). Repeated, not scoped.
(3) "A citation establishes it" - none attaches. The only bitsandbytes-adjacent reference is Dettmers et al., QLoRA (11_references.txt:67), which introduces NF4 and its CUDA kernels but cannot establish a durable capability claim about later releases of the library.
(4) "It is a definition" - no, it is an empirical claim about third-party software.

DECISIVE EVIDENCE: the report cannot even fall back on "the version we pinned". Table 5.2 in Chapter 5 lists Python 3.11.15, torch 2.11.0+cu130 and transformers 5.5.0, but for bitsandbytes records only "(installed; NF4 support verified)" - no version at all. And /Users/tanueihorng/fyp_quant/requirements.txt:9 is an open lower bound, "bitsandbytes>=0.43.0", not a pin. So the one qualification that would make the sentence true-as-scoped is missing from the artifact. The loader's own error string ("bitsandbytes quantized loading requires CUDA.") carries the same unqualified wording, so the codebase provides no scoped source either.

SEVERITY: low; no result depends on it. The fix adds rigour rather than deleting content: rescope to e.g. "...because the bitsandbytes build in this environment supports four-bit loading only on CUDA, and the loader therefore refuses to quantize on a CPU runtime", and record the actual bitsandbytes version in Table 5.2. Both Ch. 3.3 and the Ch. 4 restatement (and optionally the loader.py:222 message) should be changed together.

sentence: This prevents accidental CPU execution of a four-bit path that BitsAndBytes does not support.
cited: No citation attached; the reference list contains QLoRA and LLM.int8() but neither is cited here.
why_unsupported: An unqualified statement about a third-party library's capability across all versions and backends. bitsandbytes' multi-backend work has added non-CUDA (including CPU) execution paths for 4-bit, so the blanket "does not support" is version- and build-dependent, and the study measured nothing about CPU 4-bit support — it simply refuses to run there.
proposed_fix: "This prevents accidental CPU execution of the four-bit path, which the CUDA bitsandbytes build pinned in this study does not provide." — scope the claim to the pinned build rather than to the library in general.

verdict.reasoning:
I tried to refute this and could not. All four escape routes close:

(1) "It's about the study's own design." Partly, but the load-bearing clause isn't. The DESIGN fact is the PRECEDING sentence — "the loader raises a clear RuntimeError if quantized is true but the resolved runtime device is not cuda" (04_chapter_4, line 77), which matches the code exactly (ethical_benchmark/models/loader.py:220-223). The flagged sentence is the external JUSTIFICATION for that guard, and its content is a proposition about a third-party library's capability, not an observation of the study's system. The study never exercised a CPU four-bit path; it refuses to enter one, which measures nothing about whether the path exists.

(2) "Already hedged/scoped." No — and I checked hard for a scoping anchor. The sentence is unqualified present tense with no version, build, or backend qualifier. Critically, the report's own environment table (05_chapter_5, ~line 97) pins Python 3.11.15, torch 2.11.0+cu130 and transformers 5.5.0 but leaves the bitsandbytes version cell as "(installed; NF4 support verified)" — the one library the claim is about is the one library with no version pinned. requirements.txt:9 carries an open-ended `bitsandbytes>=0.43.0`, spanning both the CUDA-only era and the multi-backend era. So nothing anywhere in the document scopes the assertion to a build where it holds. Nor is it a one-off shorthand: 03_chapter_3_methodology line 109 repeats it independently — "the CPU path is not used for quantized runs, because BitsAndBytes requires a CUDA device."

(3) "A citation establishes it." Nothing is cited at that sentence. The only bnb-adjacent reference is [32] Dettmers et al., QLoRA (11_references, line 67), annotated "(Introduces NF4 and the bitsandbytes integration.)" — it establishes what NF4 is, not the non-existence of non-CUDA backends, and it predates the multi-backend work entirely. This is exactly the D56 failure mode: a real, correctly formatted reference that does not entail the sentence near it.

(4) "It's a definition." No. The glossary (17_appendix_f) defines BNB as "Library providing the NF4 four-bit quantization integration used by Hugging Face transformers" — no CUDA exclusivity in the definition, so the sentence is not restating one.

On substance, the auditor is right that the claim is build-dependent: bitsandbytes' multi-backend refactor shipped non-CUDA execution paths (CPU, Intel XPU, ROCm), with CPU NF4 inference reaching official support in the 0.47 line — inside the `>=0.43.0` band the repo permits, and well behind the torch 2.11 / transformers 5.5 stack the report describes. So the blanket claim is at best version-dependent and quite possibly false for the very environment documented in Chapter 5.

Severity is LOW and non-conclusion-touching: this is implementation rationale in Chapter 4, and no result in Chapters 6-7 rests on it. The guard itself remains fully defensible on other grounds. Per D56's "prefer the fix that adds rigour," the remediation is a hedge, not a deletion — state what is actually true of the study ("quantized runs in this study are CUDA-only by design; the loader refuses CPU quantized loading rather than silently entering an unvalidated path") or scope it to the build ("the CUDA-targeted bitsandbytes build used here provides no supported CPU four-bit path"). Remediation should cover BOTH instances: 04_chapter_4 line 77 and 03_chapter_3 line 109. Note the loader's own error string ("bitsandbytes quantized loading requires CUDA.") carries the same unqualified assertion; it is user-facing, not a report claim, so it is optional to touch, but the report sentences are the ones under audit.

One fairness caveat on the finding as written: the auditor's phrasing implies CPU 4-bit is broadly available, which overstates maturity for early multi-backend releases. That does not rescue the sentence — the defect is the total absence of a qualifier, not the exact version boundary — but the remediation should hedge rather than assert the converse.

sentence: The answer to RQ1 is therefore scorer-dependent in the sense that a weaker scorer would have produced a different headline, and the scorer selected here is the one that agrees best with human annotators.
defect_class: (c) superlative / exclusivity, generalised from a single non-independent annotator
why_unsupported: "Human annotators" (plural) rests on one annotator, the study's author, on a 200-item stratified subset that deliberately over-samples disagreement cases (line 789); a second annotator remains open work. Only two of the four scorers used (classifier, regex) were compared against human labels at all, so "the one that agrees best" is a superlative over a two-item comparison presented as a general ranking. The preceding sentence's "The scorer question is settled against human judgment rather than by assertion" overstates the same evidence.
proposed_fix: "...and of the two scorers compared against human labels, the classifier agreed substantially better with the single (author) annotator on a 200-item stratified subset (kappa 0.59 vs 0.11). A second annotator has not yet been run." Correspondingly soften "settled" to "weighed against human labels rather than by assertion".

verdict.reasoning:
I could not refute this finding. Checked all four refutation routes and each fails.

**1. "It's about the study's own data/design."** True but not exculpatory. The complaint is not that a world-claim lacks a citation — it is that the sentence mis-describes the study's *own* design. Every other place in the report gets it right: Ch 6 line 789 ("a single human annotator, the study's author"), Ch 7 line 29 ("that is a moderate, single-annotator agreement"), Ch 9 line 21 ("Because that grounding rests on a single annotator"), Appendix I.4 ("this is a single annotator on a partly subjective rubric"). The RQ7 synthesis sentence is the one place that pluralizes to "human annotators," and the plural matters because the sole annotator is the author — non-independent, and a second annotator is carried as open work (T30b). Plural implies multiple raters, i.e. exactly the inter-rater grounding the study explicitly does not have.

**2. "Adequately hedged/scoped by neighbours."** This is the strongest defence and it does not hold. The preceding sentence says "against human labels" with no annotator count, so nothing in the paragraph corrects the plural. Worse, the sentence immediately before the superlative introduces two *additional* scorers ("A second frontier judge and an open-weight guard model"), which widens rather than narrows the apparent comparison set. I verified by grep that neither gpt-4o nor LlamaGuard was ever scored against human labels — both were compared only against the classifier (κ 0.68–0.95 and κ 0.36–0.92). Appendix I.4 confirms the human comparison set is exactly two automated scorers: "Of the three scorers the human applied the highest bar ... 37 of 200, against the classifier's 46 and the regex's 132." So "the one that agrees best with human annotators" is a superlative over a 2-of-4 comparison, presented immediately after naming the other two as a general ranking.

**3. "A citation establishes it."** No citation is attached to the sentence.

**4. "It's a definition."** No — it is an empirical claim about relative scorer-human agreement.

**Additional support the auditor found but understated:** the preceding sentence's "settled" is contradicted by the report's own appendix. I.4 states the κ values "are computed on a harder-than-representative slice and are not population estimates," that "the direction in which a representative population would move them is not identified by this design," and that "κ = 0.59 makes the classifier a better scorer rather than a perfect human proxy." "Settled" over-states a disagreement-enriched (120/200), single-rater, moderate-κ comparison that the appendix itself declines to generalise.

**Where I'd temper the auditor:** the substantive ordering claim is sound and survives the sampling design — Appendix I.4 says so explicitly ("What does survive that sampling is the ordering and its size"). The classifier really does beat the regex against the human by a wide margin (precision 61% vs 23%; 18 false-harmful calls vs 101). So this is not conclusion-touching; RQ1's null is unaffected. The defect is confined to wording in the synthesis paragraph: the plural "annotators" from n=1, the unbounded superlative "the one that agrees best" over an incomplete comparison, and "settled." This is the classic pattern the project's own D56 rule targets — a careful caveat stated correctly in the detail sections and dropped in the headline summary. Clear enough to report; the fix is a sentence rewrite (e.g. "the scorer selected here is the one of the two that agrees better with the study's single human annotator"), not a re-analysis.

sentence: A team that validates on the full-precision 1.7B release and ships the 4-bit build should expect a lower capability level than they signed off on (−9.0 pp MMLU) rather than a higher harmful-compliance rate.
defect_class: (f) non-significant result converted into a prediction of no effect
cited: No citation attached (it is a deployment prediction, not a literature claim).
why_unsupported: The "rather than a higher harmful-compliance rate" clause turns a null ΔASR into an affirmative expectation of no harm increase, and projects it onto arbitrary deployments. The study measured no significant ASR increase under direct requests, at one budget, on a fixed prompt set, with the acknowledged MDE of a 400-prompt paired design — which does not license telling a deployer they should not expect one. The −9.0 pp figure is also a zero-shot MMLU-subset delta, not a general "capability level".
proposed_fix: "A team that validates on the full-precision 1.7B release and ships the 4-bit build should expect a materially lower capability level than they signed off on (−9.0 pp on this study's zero-shot MMLU subset). This study found no significant change in harmful compliance under direct requests, but a non-significant result at this sample size does not establish that none occurs."

verdict.reasoning:
CONFIRMED, but narrower than the auditor stated. I attempted refutation on all three offered grounds and only the core (f) charge survives.

Chapter 8 (`build_fyp_report_v6.js:1152`, mirrored at `build_fyp_report_v5.js:1022`) converts that into "the artefact does not affect **any result** reported here," dropping the "two counts" bound while widening the quantifier. **Levers 3 and 4** — no citation is attached to the sentence, and it is not a definition.

**Substantively, the two-pronged argument does not reach the universal:**

1. *Self-contradiction within the same sentence-pair.* The paragraph states "It inflates response length" — and response length is a reported result: "the median HarmBench response is 1,675 characters against 567 at 128" (Ch. 8 ¶17 and Appendix I.12). The ≈62 percent "character-ceiling proxy" truncation figure is likewise a length-ceiling statistic, and responses hitting the ceiling is exactly what the missing turn-end stop causes ("responses frequently run to the full token budget"). So the artefact affects at least one reported number by the sentence's own admission.

2. *The premise "produced identically by both pair members, so its effect is matched across the pair by construction" is itself unmeasured and cuts against report evidence.* Chapter 8's MMLU paragraph documents that answer-format artefacts are strongly pair-**asymmetric**: the lenient fallback parser fires on 48.7% of the 4-bit member's MMLU items against 3.3% at fp16 (52.3% vs 2.5% on ARC). Format degradation is concentrated in the 4-bit member, so "identical by construction" is an assumption, not a fact — and 4-bit members being more format-broken is a reason to expect *more* run-on, not equal run-on.

3. *The classifier prong is HarmBench-only, but the artefact is loop-wide.* "The primary classifier scores the whole response" covers judge-scored HarmBench ASR and nothing else. I detected the artefact's actual signature in `/Users/tanueihorng/fyp_quant/results_512/<alias>/harmbench/raw.jsonl` (refusal, then a fabricated user turn — "I understand. CORROBORATION INSIDE THE DOCUMENT

Chapter 8 itself measures a closely analogous decoding/format artefact and finds it grossly asymmetric across the same pairing: the lenient MMLU fallback parser fires on 48.7% of the 4-bit member's items against 3.3% at fp16, and 52.3% vs 2.5% on ARC. The report therefore already demonstrates that format-level generation behaviour is not matched across pair members, which is the premise this sentence assumes without checking.

- The paragraph's *second* argument is sound and independent: "the primary classifier scores the whole response rather than just its opening, so a continuation that emitted harmful content would still be counted." That is what actually protects the ASR measurement, and it needs no symmetry assumption. The conclusion ("does not affect any result reported here") is plausibly still correct — it is the stated warrant that is unsupported, so the fix is to replace the false leg, not to delete the limitation.
- My detector is a recall-limited regex keyed to the phrasings visible in the Phi examples, so absolute rates are floors and the zeros for other families could under-count. verdict.reasoning:
I tried each of the four refutation routes and none of them closes.

**Route 1 — "it's about the study's own data."** Partly true and this is the best defence available: "The data therefore..." follows an enumeration of the five per-pair ΔASR values, and the very next sentence says "NF4," which lends some contextual scoping. But the OBJECT of the verb is a general proposition about quantization, not a description of the study's data. And the sentence writes "quantization" unqualified, while Chapter 7 explicitly bounds the findings: "findings are bounded to BitsAndBytes on-the-fly quantization... Alternative methods such as GPTQ, AWQ, and the GGUF family... may produce different effects... The present study does not claim to characterise those methods." Chapter 8 further scopes every harmful-compliance finding, "including the headline null," to direct requests only. The conclusion sentence claims refutation over a scope the report itself disclaims two chapters earlier.

**Route 2 — "already adequately hedged and scoped."** No, and this is the sharpest evidence. The parallel sentence in Appendix I (19_appendix_i…, line 185) carries BOTH qualifiers the conclusion drops: "the optimistic narrative that **NF4** quantization is a clean safety win **in this scale range**." The scoping exists elsewhere in the same document and was lost here. Note also the verb asymmetry inside the same two-sentence pair: "refute" toward the optimistic side vs. "give no evidence that NF4 significantly erodes guardrails **at the reference budget**" toward the pessimistic side — same data, one direction gets a strong verb and no scope, the other gets a hedged verb and a scope tag.

**Route 3 — "a citation establishes it."** No citation on the sentence, and I swept every chapter. The report's literature review documents three positions on quantization and safety: degradation (Kharinaev [10], Q-resafe [36], Egashira [12]), non-uniform direction (HarmLevelBench [35]), and preservation (Hong et al. [37], "4-bit quantization broadly preserves trustworthiness"). None is an optimistic improvement claim. The report itself calls [37] "the nearest prior analogue to the null-safety-at-four-bit picture found here" — i.e. an ally of the finding, not the opponent being refuted. So the opponent position is not documented anywhere in the report, in any chapter, with or without a source. The reader cannot check that anyone holds it.

**Route 4 — definition.** No, it is an empirical inferential claim.

**On the auditor's reasoning, one correction.** Prong (f) as written ("non-replication in five pairs is failure to support, not refutation") is too blunt: refuting a *reliability* claim is a genuinely lower bar than establishing an effect, since "reliably" is a claim about consistency across cases and the study observed the deltas straddling zero (−0.040 to +0.040). That part of the auditor's argument is weaker than they think. But the defect survives on the report's OWN stated epistemic standard: Appendix I line 15 says "the claim established here is 'no detectable change at n = 200' rather than a proven zero." Four of the five pairs contribute non-detections, and with an MDE of 0.04–0.09 a small consistent improvement is not excluded. The sentence converts four non-detections into positive disproof, which is exactly the inference the report elsewhere refuses to make.

**Verdict: finding stands**, on grounds (i) unsourced attribution of an opponent position the report's own literature review never documents, (ii) unqualified "quantization" exceeding the Chapter 7/8 bounds (BitsAndBytes NF4, direct requests, one budget), and (iii) "refute" exceeding the report's own non-detection-is-not-proven-zero standard.
